title: Ending On-Call Nightmares: Architectural Lessons from Distributed Caching with Apache Ignite
body_text: Written By: Shreyas Bhandare The Nightmare Picture this: It’s Friday evening, you’re on-call, and your entire in-memory Apache Ignite cluster just went down. A simple data streamer that consumes data from Kafka and puts it into Ignite crashed. Why did a single data streamer take down the entire cluster? Apache Ignite 2.15 introduced a complicated bug that broke existing security contexts. This happened to us. To give some background, we built a mission-critical caching layer on Apache Ignite to replace legacy cache services. The cluster stores billions of off-heap records, amounting to a couple of hundred gigabytes and ingests a high volume of real-time updates streamed from Kafka. Through Ignite’s Continuous Query, about 500 upstream hosts always receive fresh data. We had a clean, separated architecture: Ignite Cluster: Kubernetes StatefulSets running on server nodes that host our caching layer. Streamers: Kubernetes Deployments running our Kafka consumers. Streamers are a part of the Ignite cluster as thick clients. This worked beautifully until we migrated to Ignite 2.15. After the upgrade, even a routine streamer restart — due to deployments, pod evictions or GKE upgrades — could trigger node crashes, causing server pods to enter an error loop with the exception: JVM will be halted immediately due to the failure: [failureCtx=FailureContext [type=SYSTEM_WORKER_TERMINATION, err=java.lang.IllegalStateException: Failed to find security context for subject with given ID] An Operational Breaking Point What started as an occasional on-call scare quickly became an operational hazard: Random cluster deaths: Routine streamer deployments turned into Russian roulette, and any restart could take down server nodes. Security context exceptions: Server pods repeatedly fell into the same error loop, requiring remediation steps to restore stability. Outages : Each incident required cluster recovery, which at times was extensive. Deployment paralysis: Releases required careful coordination due to deployment instability. Data loss: When enough nodes failed, upstream data freshness was temporarily impacted. Operational overhead: We had to maintain two Ignite clusters in each region as a fallback during deployments. We implemented additional redundancy measures to support safe deployments. One may wonder… was upgrading to version 2.15 really necessary? In our case, the other extensive bug fixes, new features and enhancements in 2.15 clearly outweighed the benefits of staying on 2.14. And, as with any other engineering team at DV, we performed thorough due diligence, running comprehensive stress and chaos tests across all environments before proceeding with the upgrade. As we investigated further, we realized we weren’t the only ones fighting this fire. Understanding the Systemic Issue Apache Ignite’s IGNITE-21737 documents this exact issue: thick clients with security enabled can cause server nodes to become unresponsive during client disconnections. The security context validation gets stuck in loops, essentially freezing the entire server node. It was a systemic issue affecting anyone using thick clients with security enabled in Ignite 2.15+. At this point, the next logical question was: how do we fix it? Architectural Shift The primary reason for using Thick Client Streamers was their low overhead. The original solution leveraged Apache Ignite’s built-in IgniteDataStreamer and StreamAdapter , where the addMessage() method handled populating the Ignite cache. Since this option was provided out of the box by Ignite, we just had to implement our Kafka consumers around it, keeping the overall design simple. Before committing to an architectural turnaround, we tried every reasonable alternative. We experimented with quick bug fixes, adjusted our security plugin, added defensive guards around client disconnects and explored custom failure handlers. None of it addressed the real problem, because the failure pattern didn’t originate in our streamer logic or infrastructure. No amount of defensive coding could prevent it. And so, it became clear: as long as our streamers connected as thick clients, the cluster would remain unstable. The only reliable solution was to remove this dependency altogether, shifting the streamers to thin clients, which avoided the problematic server-side security context handling entirely. This change also gave us several additional advantages: But moving to thin clients wasn’t just a configuration flip. It fundamentally changed how our streamers interacted with Ignite, introducing a new set of engineering challenges. Rebuilding from the Ground Up Things got a little complicated when we decided to migrate the data streamers to thin clients. The existing utility classes weren’t compatible out of the box, which meant we had to build a significant amount of custom integration logic to achieve the same functionality. We also had to rebuild resilience from scratch. Because thin clients don’t participate in cluster events, we could no longer depend on Ignite’s internal signals to detect failures or restart streamers. Instead, we developed our own health-check probes that continuously monitored client connectivity and consumer thread health, triggering safe, automated restarts whenever a disconnection occurred. With these challenges laid out, we moved on to designing and implementing the new streaming pipeline. The Technical Journey There were three steps to implement the whole migration process. Step One: Building the Thin Client Streamer logic We developed a new streamer class that leveraged Ignite’s thin client APIs to connect to our StatefulSets. The key innovation was partition-based buffering: instead of processing all records at once, we grouped incoming Kafka messages by partition and flushed them in controlled batches. This strategy helped prevent cluster overload while maintaining high throughput. We also plugged in Ignite’s partition awareness feature, which was supported out of the box. This allowed thin clients to route data requests directly to the server nodes that own the relevant data partitions, resulting in faster writes. A multi-threaded model allowed us to consume from multiple Kafka partitions in parallel. Each thread maintained its own IgniteClient instance to efficiently write data to the cache using putAll() and removeAll() . We validated that the behavior of putAll() and removeAll() closely matched our original IgniteDataStreamer implementation, meaning that during a full data load, the thick-client streamer and thin-client streamer performed exactly the same. To continuously monitor performance, we added Prometheus summary metrics to track throughput and latency over time. On full data load, the thick-client streamer and thin-client streamer performed exactly the same. To ensure reliability, we also built in safeguards for edge cases, including retry mechanisms, rollback handling for failed Ignite writes, and recovery logic for Kafka offset commit failures. Step Two: Health Monitoring Infrastructure We built our own monitoring, and being on Kubernetes helped us build an easy and workable solution: Check if Kafka Consumer Threads are healthy Check if IgniteClients are healthy If any of the above fail, restart the data streamer after a delay Step Three: Moving Actual Datasets This was the moment of truth: switching our real datasets to use the new thin-client streamer. The beauty of our approach was that it required only configuration changes — no code changes for individual datasets, just Helm chart updates and property file modifications. We could migrate datasets one by one, testing each one before moving to the next. What Made This Work This approach completely sidestepped the security context issue. Since thin clients don’t create the same security context dependencies as thick clients, the Ignite server nodes don’t get stuck in error loops. When we restart a streamer deployment, it’s just a regular client disconnect/reconnect, meaning no impact on server nodes. Recall the earlier separated-architecture diagram. Moving to thin clients allowed us to decouple the system even further: An Absolute Operational Win After we went live, the results were positive and immediate. Earlier, we used to spend two to six hours per incident, sometimes multiple incidents per month. It went down to zero. There were significant operational improvements as well. We could deploy streamers and server nodes with 100% confidence. GKE upgrades no longer need careful scheduling. The person on-call would spend time improving monitoring and alerts rather than firefighting the Ignite cluster outages. Thanks to the new health check probes, we eliminated the need to call SRE support for any manual intervention. Looking Back from the Other Side We found that Ignite security contexts can fail in severe and unexpected ways, and that connection type plays a critical role in overall cluster stability. We also discovered that thin clients are far more capable than we had previously assumed — something we had never fully explored in the past. Ultimately, the most effective solution wasn’t a patch or waiting for a new Ignite release, but an architectural shift that addressed the root cause at the connection layer. Today, this architecture powers DV’s low-latency, high-throughput platform, processing hundreds of billions of pre-bid requests daily across multiple DSPs while consistently meeting strict SLAs. It has transformed our streaming pipeline into a resilient and stable foundation we can fully rely on. Ending On-Call Nightmares: Architectural Lessons from Distributed Caching with Apache Ignite was originally published in DoubleVerify Engineering on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: How To Become an Electrical Technician: A Step-by-Step Guide
summary: Want to become an electrical technician? This guide breaks down hands-on skills training, NCCER credential opportunities and other key requirements for this career path.
body_text: Electrical careers can get confusing fast. Technician, electrician, electronics, robotics, industrial maintenance and wind energy roles can all involve electrical systems, but they don’t always follow the same path . If you’re trying to figure out how to become an electrical technician, start by understanding the role itself. That difference matters when you are choosing hands-on career training. Universal Technical Institute (UTI) offers several electrical training options tied to different career paths, including electronics, robotics and automation, industrial maintenance and wind energy.130 Comparing these paths can help students narrow in on the systems, tools and work environments that fit them best. Note: UTI’s electrical programs do not prepare graduates for employment as electricians, and graduates will not be eligible for certification as an electrician without additional training and meeting state licensing requirements. Becoming a licensed electrician usually requires completing additional state-specific steps, including apprenticeship hours and exams. This guide breaks down what electrical technicians do, how they differ from electricians, what skills they use, how credentials from organizations such as the National Center for Construction Education & Research (NCCER) can fit into training, and how to start planning your next move. What Does an Electrical Technician Do? An electrical technician installs, tests, maintains and troubleshoots electrical and electronic systems across industrial, commercial and technical environments. The work can vary by industry. Some technicians work with panels, circuits and access control systems. Others work with industrial machinery, robotics, automation systems , wind turbine systems or field-service equipment . Electrical technician roles are often practical and problem-based. A technician needs to understand what a system is supposed to do, test it safely, find what is wrong, and document the repair or next step. Task type What it can involve Test Circuits, components, control systems and meters. Troubleshoot Faults, failed components, inconsistent power and system errors. Maintain Equipment, panels, machines and electrical systems. Document Readings, repairs, safety checks and service notes. Common electrical technician work environments Electrical technician work can look different depending on the systems, equipment and industry involved. Industrial facilities: Technicians may help maintain machinery, motors, control systems and electrical equipment used in production environments. Automation environments: Technicians may work with robotics, sensors, controls, motors and programmable systems that help equipment run in sequence. Wind energy : Technicians may support electrical and mechanical systems inside wind turbine technology, including components tied to power generation and field service. Security and access control: Technicians may help install, test or service electronic security systems, alarms, cameras or access control equipment. Skills electrical technicians use Electrical technicians draw on a mix of electrical safety knowledge, technical theory and hands-on diagnostic skills, including: Safety and lockout/tagout awareness Electrical theory Wiring and circuit basics Digital multimeter use Blueprint and schematic reading Troubleshooting and documentation Mechanical and electrical system thinking To pursue this type of career, you do not need to know all of this on day one. That is what training is for. Read : Preventive Maintenance for Electrical Systems: Key Technician Skills Electrical Technician vs. Electrician: What’s the Difference? Electrical technicians and electricians may both work with electrical systems, but they are not the same role . The table below breaks down the biggest differences in job focus, training path, work settings and licensing. Category Electrical Technician Electrician Main focus Testing, troubleshooting and maintaining electrical or electronic systems. Installing and repairing electrical wiring or systems in buildings. Training path Trade school, technical training or employer training. Apprenticeship, required hours and state or local licensing. Work settings Industrial, manufacturing, energy, automation and field service. Residential, commercial, and industrial construction or service. Licensing Varies by role, employer and state. Usually required by state or local rules. Electrical technician roles can be broader and may focus on systems, equipment and troubleshooting across different industries. Electrician roles are more likely to involve formal licensing requirements, so double-check local and state rules if your goal is to become an electrician. Why this difference matters before choosing training UTI’s Electrical & Electronics programs prepare students for entry-level technician roles after graduating.130 Electrician licensing, which typically requires apprenticeship hours and state approval, is a separate path with its own requirements. This is why it helps to separate technician training from electrician licensing early. Electrical technician training may help students build useful electrical skills, but electrician licensure has its own rules, timelines and state-specific requirements. Read : Electrical Certification: Purpose, Process & Value Step 1 : Choose the Electrical Career Path You Want Electrical technician training can lead toward different types of hands-on work. The sections below compare common directions by interests, equipment, possible roles and UTI’s electrical training options. Electronics and industrial systems This path is for students interested in electrical components, industrial systems, wiring fundamentals and troubleshooting. Best fit if you like: Wiring, electronics, panels, access control systems and hands-on troubleshooting. For those who want to work with: Electrical components, meters, circuits, fire alarm systems, security systems and access control equipment. Possible paths: Electrical technician, electrician’s assistant, fire alarm technician, security systems technician or cable technician.77 Electrical, Electronics, & Industrial Technology career training UTI’s Electrical, Electronics, & Industrial Technology program is the broadest electrical systems path in the electrical training suite. It focuses on fundamentals students can use around electrical circuits, electronic components, wiring, meters, fire alarm systems, security systems and troubleshooting. This program can be a fit for students who want to understand how electrical and electronic systems work before pursuing entry-level roles tied to installation support, security/access control or related technical environments after graduating. Robotics and automation This path applies electrical training to automated systems that rely on controls, sensors, motors and diagnostics. It is built for students who want to understand how electrical systems help machines move, respond and repeat tasks. Best fit if you like: Robotics, automated systems, controls, sensors and machine movement. For those who want to work with: Motors, sensors, programmable systems, automation equipment, control panels and diagnostic tools. Possible paths: Mechatronics technician, automation technician, robotics technician or maintenance-related roles, depending on employer requirements.77 Electrical, Robotics & Automation Technology career training UTI’s electrical, robotics and automation training focuses on the electrical side of robotics, automation and industrial technology. Students can build skills tied to controls, sensors, motors, diagnostics, automated equipment and system-level troubleshooting. This program can be a fit for students who want electrical training connected to robotics and automation environments, not just general wiring or electronics. Read : How PLC Programming Powers Modern Automated Systems Industrial maintenance This path connects electrical training to industrial machinery, maintenance systems and equipment uptime. It can include motors, controls, troubleshooting, mechanical systems and the crossover between electrical and industrial work. Best fit if you like: Solving equipment problems, working around machinery and helping systems stay running. For those who want to work with: Motors, controls, electrical systems, mechanical systems, industrial equipment and maintenance procedures. Possible paths: Industrial maintenance technician, maintenance technician, plant technician or field service technician, depending on employer needs.77 The demand for energy/industrial maintenance technicians is strong. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, employment is projected to grow 16% from 2024 to 2034.64 Electrical & Industrial Maintenance Technology career training UTI’s electrical and industrial maintenance training connects electrical skills to the equipment used in industrial and facility environments. Students can learn about motors, mechanical systems, electrical systems, maintenance procedures, troubleshooting and industrial technology. This program can be a fit for students who like the idea of diagnosing problems, maintaining machinery, and working across both electrical and mechanical systems. Read : Is Industrial Maintenance a Good Career Path? Wind energy This path focuses on electrical training in wind turbine technology and renewable energy systems. It can include turbine systems, electrical/mechanical components, diagnostics, field-service readiness and safety in turbine-related environments. Best fit if you like: Renewable energy, turbine technology, field service and hands-on electrical/mechanical work. For those who want to work with: Turbine systems, electrical components, mechanical systems, safety procedures and diagnostic tools. Possible paths: Wind turbine technician or field-service roles, depending on employer requirements.77 The demand for wind turbine technicians is strong. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, employment is projected to grow 50% from 2024 to 2034.63 Electrical & Wind Turbine Technology career training UTI’s electrical and wind training connects electrical skills to turbine systems, renewable energy technology and field-service environments. Students can learn about electrical systems, mechanical systems, turbine technology, diagnostics and safety practices tied to wind energy work. This program can be a fit for students who want electrical training connected to renewable energy and turbine systems rather than a building-wiring path. Read : The Most In-Demand Skills for Wind Turbine Technicians in 2026 Step 2 : Build the Core Skills Electrical Technicians Use Electrical technician work starts with safety and basic theory, then builds toward tools, diagrams and troubleshooting. Each skill helps technicians understand not just what is happening in a system, but how to find and fix problems. Electrical safety Safety is the first skill, not an afterthought. Electrical systems can create serious hazards, so technicians need disciplined habits that result in safe practices. Electrical safety also connects to real job tasks like testing circuits, working near panels, maintaining equipment or confirming that a system is safe to inspect. Electrical safety skills can include: Identifying hazards. Using electrical personal protective equipment (PPE). Confirming equipment is de-energized. Following workplace safety procedures . Understanding lockout/tagout awareness. Electrical theory Electrical theory covers concepts like voltage, current, resistance, circuits and power flow. These ideas help technicians understand how electrical components work together. Theoretical electrical concepts can’t be learned by just memorizing terms. It helps technicians understand what normal system behavior should look like, so they can recognize when something is wrong. Read : Voltage Drop Test: Key Concepts & How To Do It Tools, meters and diagnostic equipment Once students understand basic electrical ideas, they need to learn how to measure, test and inspect systems safely. Tools help technicians turn a problem into evidence, whether they are checking voltage, confirming continuity or narrowing down where a fault may be happening. Digital multimeters: Measuring voltage, resistance and continuity. Hand tools: Supporting wiring, installation, adjustment and repair tasks. Testing equipment: Helping technicians confirm whether components and circuits are working as expected. Panels and components: Giving students practice with real electrical system layouts, protection devices and connection points. Schematics and diagrams Beginners may see wires, symbols and panels as overwhelming. Training can help them learn how to follow the logic of a system. Schematics help technicians see how parts connect. They can also help technicians locate components, understand circuit paths and troubleshoot more efficiently. Troubleshooting Troubleshooting is where safety, theory, tools and diagrams come together. Instead of guessing, technicians use a step-by-step process. A simple electrical troubleshooting sequence may look like this: Identify the issue. Review the system or diagram. Test safely. Compare readings to expected behavior. Narrow down the cause. Document or communicate the fix. Real equipment practice Hands-on practice helps students move from learning concepts to applying them. This matters because electrical work often depends on reading a system, choosing the right tool and making a safe decision. In lab settings, students may practice with electrical panels, digital multimeters, circuit protection devices, sensors, motors and diagnostic systems, depending on the program. That kind of practice helps students connect classroom concepts to the way electrical systems behave in real-world environments. Once you understand the core skills, the next step is choosing the training route that helps you build those skills. Read : Trade School vs. Traditional Classroom: Which Offers More Hands-On Training? Step 3 : Get Electrical Technician Training Electrical technician training can start in high school, continue through technical training and keep developing on the job. The best route depends on the kind of electrical work you want to pursue, the employer’s requirements, and whether licensing or certification is involved. High school preparation High school students can start building useful habits early, but beginners can still enter training later without having learned these subjects first. Helpful classes and activities include: Math and physics. Electronics or robotics electives. Shop or computer classes. Mechanical hobbies or projects. These experiences can help students get comfortable with problem-solving, tools, systems and technical thinking before entering a training program. Many trade schools, like UTI, and entry-level industry roles require a high school diploma, GED or equivalent, so students should review admissions requirements and job postings early. Read : Trade School vs. 4-Year College After High School: Which Path Makes Sense? Trade school or technical training Trade school or technical training can give students a structured way to build job-relevant electrical skills before applying for entry-level roles. This can be especially helpful for beginners who want guided practice with tools, electrical concepts and troubleshooting before entering the job market. What to look for in an electrical technician training program: Hands-on training focus . Electrical safety and theory. Tools, meters and diagnostic practice. Troubleshooting-focused coursework. Training tied to real equipment or systems. Industry-recognized credential opportunities, such as NCCER credentials, if available. Job search support . Clear information about what roles the program is designed to prepare students for. Students should compare programs based on the electrical path they want to pursue. Electronics, robotics, industrial maintenance and wind energy all involve electrical skills, but they can point toward different tools, work settings and job titles. On-the-job training Even after technical training, electrical technicians continue learning on the job because every employer uses different systems, equipment and procedures. Training can help you build the foundation, but employers will train you on their specific systems, safety processes, tools, software or equipment. On-the-job training may cover: Employer-specific equipment. Company safety procedures. Documentation and reporting systems. Specialized tools or software. Site-specific troubleshooting processes. Team workflows and service expectations. Once you understand the main training routes, you should look at whether your target role requires certifications, licensing or additional employer qualifications. Read : What to Expect in Your First Year of Electrical Training Step 4: Understand Certification and Licensing Requirements Certification and licensing are not the same thing. Which one matters depends on the role, employer, state and type of electrical work. Certifications and credentials for electrical technicians Certifications are not always required for electrical technician roles. Some employers or specialties may prefer or require credentials, especially when a role involves safety procedures, electrical systems, specialized equipment or industrial environments. At UTI, students in our electrical training programs have the opportunity to earn NCCER credentials as they train. NCCER credentials can help validate training tied to construction basics, electrical fundamentals, wiring, safety and electronic systems. Credentials may matter for: Safety training. Electrical fundamentals. Construction-focused skills. Low-voltage or electronic systems. Industrial or facility-specific work environments. Employer-preferred qualifications. Check job postings for the roles you want to pursue after training. That is the fastest way to understand what a specific employer expects. Read : How Do You Get NCCER Certified? A Step-by-Step Guide Licensing for electrical technicians Licensing requirements for electrical technician roles vary by location, employer and job duties. Some technician roles may not require a license, while others may involve regulated tasks depending on the state or local jurisdiction. Requirements can also change if the role involves electrical installation, code-related work or work that overlaps with electrician duties. Before choosing a program or applying for a role, students should check state and local requirements for the specific job title and region they are targeting. What if I want to become a licensed electrician? If your goal is electrician licensure, that is a separate path from electrical technician training. Research your state’s apprenticeship, work-hour and licensing requirements before choosing a program. UTI’s Electrical & Electronic programs are designed to prepare students for entry-level roles using the provided training, not electrician licensure. Students who want to become licensed electricians should confirm what education, apprenticeship hours, exams, and state or local approvals may apply to their target path. Read : Why the Skilled Trades Shortage is Creating Opportunities Step 5: Apply for Entry-Level Electrical Technician Roles Training gives you a foundation, but the next step is knowing what roles match that foundation. Job titles differ by employer, industry and location, so search broadly and read descriptions closely. Entry-level job titles to search for After training, graduates can use entry-level job titles as starting points for their search. Because titles vary, they should search broadly and check each description for duties, requirements and experience level. Pathway Entry-level job titles to search Electrical and electronics Electrical technician, electrician’s assistant, fire alarm technician, security systems technician, cable technician, mechatronics technician Robotics and automation Robotics & automation technician, field service technician, control systems technician, machine specialist, controls engineer, maintenance technician Industrial maintenance Industrial maintenance technician, maintenance technician, plant technician, field service technician, installation technician Wind energy Wind turbine technician, field service technician, installation technician, tower technician, wind service technician Job titles can overlap across industries. The description will tell you whether the role actually matches your training, interests and experience level. Read : Electrician Apprenticeship vs. Trade School: Time, Cost and Career Paths How to read job descriptions Once you find a title that looks relevant, scan the posting for the actual tools, systems and requirements mentioned. Look for: Tools and voltage ranges. Schematics and troubleshooting. Safety requirements. Travel and shift expectations. Certification or experience requirements. Beginner-friendly language or training provided. If a posting mentions hands-on troubleshooting, familiar tools or beginner-friendly language, it may be worth a closer look. If it requires licensing, years of experience or advanced certifications, determine whether you qualify before applying. After identifying the right roles, the next step is translating your training into language employers recognize. How to show your skills as a beginner Early-career applicants should focus on specific tools, systems and tasks they practiced and learned. The goal is to show hands-on familiarity without overstating experience. Résumé-friendly phrasing examples include: Practiced electrical diagnostics using testing equipment. Built foundational skills in circuits, wiring and troubleshooting. Trained with electrical/mechanical systems in a lab environment. Completed hands-on electrical training using panels, meters and protection devices in a lab environment. Practiced using digital multimeters to measure voltage, resistance and continuity. Job searching gets easier when you understand the title, the description and the skills behind the work. When you’re new to the field, your experience may not come from years on the job yet. It may come from training, lab sessions, certifications, safety habits, troubleshooting practice and the way you explain those skills on a resume. UTI’s Career Services team can help students craft and optimize resumes that highlight hands-on training, technical skills and program-related knowledge. Career Services can also help students with limited or no industry experience find part-time, industry-related opportunities while they train, which can help them gain exposure to the field and offset training-related expenses.1 Read : 5 UTI Graduate Success Stories: From the Classroom to Career How Long Does It Take To Become an Electrical Technician? The time it takes to become an electrical technician depends on the path, program and role requirements. A simple planning path is: Choose a focus, complete training, check role requirements, apply for entry-level roles and complete employer onboarding. Training timeline Your training timeline may depend on: Program choice. Full-time vs. part-time schedule. Campus availability. Prior experience. Course sequencing or start dates. Employer requirements. Additional certifications or licensing. Apprenticeship hours, if pursuing electrician licensure. Employer-specific training. Certification prep. Background checks or onboarding steps. Relocation. Job search time. The best move is to work backward from the job title you want, then check the training, licensing and employer requirements tied to that role. Read : Want To Work in Electrical? Grants. Loans. UTI Program Good fit for students interested in Electrical, Electronics, & Industrial Technology Electronics, industrial systems, access control and electrical troubleshooting Electrical, Robotics & Automation Technology Robotics, automation, controls and automated systems Electrical & Wind Turbine Technology Wind turbines, renewable energy, field service and turbine systems Electrical & Industrial Maintenance Technology Industrial maintenance, machinery, troubleshooting and electrical/mechanical systems Once students choose a direction, the next question is what kind of training helps them build the skills behind that path. Hands-on electrical training Electrical training works best when students can connect theory to physical systems and diagnostic practice. In UTI’s Electrical & Electronics training suite, students can learn how electrical concepts show up in equipment, panels, meters, protection devices and system-level troubleshooting. Learn it: Build foundational knowledge in electrical theory, systems and safety. Test it: Practice with tools and equipment used to measure, inspect and verify electrical performance. Depending on the program, students may practice with equipment such as electrical panels, digital multimeters, circuit protection devices, motors, sensors, automation systems or turbine-related systems. title: Market timing, partnering with the right AI providers, and building your own competitive moat
summary: In the latest installment of Assembly Required, Fireflies.ai co-founder and CEO Krish Ramineni sits down with AssemblyAI founder and CEO Dylan Fox to share his insights and learnings while building a hugely popular AI-first startup
body_text: Since its founding in 2016, the AI notetaker platform Fireflies.ai has taken notes for over 16 million people and 300,000 organizations. And today, more audio is created on the Fireflies.ai platform than on Spotify each day. Krish Ramineni and his co-founder Sam Udotong created Fireflies.ai to solve a problem that was rapidly becoming universally felt: ensuring that attendees were getting maximum value out of virtual meetings and automating the cumbersome task of notetaking. At its core, the platform and its suite of AI-powered conversation intelligence tools are more about solving this human challenge than about solving a technological one. While Fireflies.ai may seem like an overnight success, Krish recalls two years when the Fireflies team worked diligently to build the right solution and find product market fit as they took a bet on the future of AI's capabilities. The recent explosion of technological advancements around automatic speech recognition, LLMs, and other frontier models is what ultimately enabled Fireflies.ai to accelerate its growth and become a dominant market leader in the AI meeting assistant space. Through a simple integration into popular virtual meeting platforms, Fireflies.ai can now automatically transcribe and summarize meetings, generate meeting notes, create action items and tasks, and so much more, empowering the next generation of remote workers. In his conversation with AssemblyAI founder and CEO Dylan Fox, Ramineni shares the unique insights he has gained while building this popular AI-first startup. Here are a few takeaways from that conversation: 1. The problem has to come first—and technology second—when thinking about solving problems for users Krish Ramineni: “It's very important not to just think about the technology first because you want to solve the problem and then figure out what technology can enable it. A lot of times going back to what you can show in a demo with these AI products is really incredible, but what you're not able to do is translate that into a real product at scale.” 2. Sometimes you have to bet on your convictions about where the market is going Krish Ramineni: “So people always like to say, oh, you guys timed the market perfectly. I always say we actually were two years too early to the market. And most people don't realize that we went through like several years of eating a lot of dirt, eating a lot of shit really, to get to where we are today...” “…But this credit really goes to my co-founder Sam, where he was bullish that, hey, the cost is going to go down, the accuracy is going to get better and when that happens, everyone's going to rush to it. We need to take that bet. And even if it's a hard problem right now, even if we're going to have to be heads down for two years, if you can just survive and lay the foundation, things will get better. You're like waiting and hoping for a better day, a better future, and it did come, but we were lucky in that sense in terms of our timing was off only by two years, not two decades.” 3. Start with figuring out how to make your customers happy, and you’ll be able to figure out how to monetize that offering Krish Ramineni: “I always like to look at three big catalysts for Fireflies. One is the speech technology getting better. That's the enabler—having really great transcriptions. The other catalyst for us was Covid. Everyone started having meetings on Zoom and Google Meet and Teams and everyone went remote. All of a sudden this new technology became front and center and people wanted to use an AI notetaker because they were just going back to back on seven Zoom calls. And then the third enabler was LLMs and then the cost of those LLMs going down. When we started working on this stuff, there was no way we could have used LLMs like GPT4 because it was too expensive. But if you look at in the last 18 months, the cost of intelligence has gone down by 95%.” “As a founder, you have all of these constraints around how do you build a business where you're balancing between quality and cost and there's like an equation. And that natural equilibrium that you reach eventually lets you get to a place where you make customers really happy and then you figure out how to monetize and how to charge for it.” 4. The true test for product market fit is if your customers find enough value out of your product that they’ll pay for it in it’s current state Dylan Fox: “Do you feel like it's gotten easier to quantify what that invisible threshold is for where things might not be good enough yet to have product market fit? Now that you guys are a bigger company and more experienced, this might be helpful for other product leaders that are building new AI products… Is it still an art where it's difficult to tell? You have to stay close to users to figure out pockets of… Oh, this is actually still like a gap where we need to find product market fit still, or have you found ways to measure for it more?” Krish Ramineni: “I mean, there's the standard ways to measure around, like, active usage and NPS and feedback. The real test is just ask the customer if they're willing to pay for it…And you'll know if it's a must have or not. I think that's really the biggest test of everything we do is this good enough for you to want to pay for it? Because I can't give this to you forever because there's a real fixed cost to this…” 5. Partnering with best-in-class AI providers lets you serve your customers better and faster, and accelerates revenue growth Krish Ramineni: “ You realize you have to make these trade-offs. Do I go spin up my own in-house models, which we've done experiments around and we have the capabilities to do, but by the time you go through one iteration cycle and get to where you need to for the market, the market has moved along. Like this is an industry where if you just blink, it changes and you will be left behind.” “So I took that decision that it's best to work with best-in-class providers of LLMs and other models and ASR and all of that and do what we do best, which is serving our customers. And there is a lot for us to do just there. And I don't think of that as being an AI wrapper or being over-reliant on other platforms because our value actually comes from how do we delight and service our users in the fastest way possible. And through that you're building your own moat. You're building incredible workflows and experiences for end users to use. Ultimately that's what makes customers happy, that's what leads to a better defensible moat and that generates more revenue for us.” 6. You have to set small, accomplishable goals to achieve what initially sounds far-fetched Krish Ramineni: “We said, look irregardless of what the outcome is, we're just going to go for 12 months and we're going to build this out and we're going to just incrementally chip away at the problem and make it better. And then, you know, one fine day you start seeing your first person that I never talked to. They go through the application, they swipe their credit card and they pay for the product and they start using it and they say good things about it or they tweet about it. And you're like, if we can get one, we can get 100. If we can get 100, I'm sure we can get to a thousand. And that's all we did. Like, we just started setting mini milestones for ourselves. In this world of AI for entrepreneurs, don't be afraid to go after something that seems technologically impossible or sounds far-fetched because you don't know what the world is going to look like one year from now, let alone five years from now.”

title: AI-native underwriting: how it works and where it differs from bolt-on AI
summary: How AI-native underwriting works end to end, and how it differs from bolt-on AI and offshore BPO.
body_text: AI-native underwriting is an approach where the intake, extraction, enrichment, and risk-scoring workflow is built around AI from the first step, with managed human review in the loop, rather than an AI feature bolted onto a workflow that was designed for manual data entry. The distinction sounds academic until you watch two carriers process the same messy submission. The AI-native platform turns a 200-tab schedule of values and a stack of carrier-specific loss runs into decision-ready data in hours. The bolt-on setup routes the same documents to a review queue, where a person still keys the hard fields by hand. This piece is a working explanation, not a pitch. It covers what AI-native underwriting means, how the pipeline actually runs end to end, and the three architectures competing for the same budget: an AI-native platform, AI bolted onto a legacy workflow, and offshore business process outsourcing (BPO). If you are trying to tell the difference between them before signing anything, the mechanics below are the part that matters. What does AI-native underwriting actually mean? AI-native underwriting means the system was designed so that AI performs the first pass on every document and every submission, and the workflow, the data model, and the review process are all shaped around that fact. The contrast is with software that was built for a manual process and later had an AI feature attached. A legacy underwriting workbench that adds an extraction button is still, underneath, a set of forms a person fills in. The AI is an assistant on the side. In an AI-native design, there is no manual-first path. The submission arrives, the model reads it, the data is structured, and a human validates the fields that need judgment. The default is machine-read; the exception is human-touched. That inversion is the whole idea, and it is why the future of commercial underwriting is described as an AI-native era rather than a feature upgrade. Two clarifications, because the term gets stretched. AI-native does not mean fully automated. It also does not mean a single large language model doing everything. Serious AI-native underwriting is a set of specialized models, insurance-specific logic, and a managed review team working together. The point is not to remove the underwriter. It is to remove the keystrokes. How does AI-native underwriting work, step by step? The workflow runs as a pipeline. Each stage produces structured output that the next stage consumes. Here is the sequence for a commercial P&C submission. Intake and clearance. The system connects to the submissions inbox, reads the email body and every attachment, classifies each document (ACORD, loss run, SOV, supplemental, driver schedule), checks the submission against coded appetite rules, flags duplicates and renewals, and chases missing documents automatically. Out-of-appetite risks are declined or flagged before an underwriter ever opens them. This front-door step is where most carriers quietly lose premium to slow intake , because the broker has already placed the deal elsewhere by the time a human gets to it. Document extraction and normalization. The model pulls structured fields out of unstructured documents and maps them to one schema, regardless of which broker or carrier produced the file. This is the part template-trained OCR cannot do at scale, and it is worth understanding why: a template-trained system learns the layout of a specific form, so a new layout breaks it. Template-agnostic extraction reads the document by meaning, so a format it has never seen still normalizes correctly. Every extracted field carries provenance back to the source, which is the difference between an AI that shows its work and one you have to trust blind . External enrichment. Based on the line of business, the system pulls relevant third-party data: license-board verification for professional liability, safety and inspection records for commercial auto, hazard data for property. The application stays the ground truth. Enrichment adds context; it does not overwrite what the applicant submitted. Risk scoring. Extracted and enriched data feed a deterministic, factor-level score. Each factor is visible and individually weighted, scored as a positive, negative, or neutral signal, so an underwriter can see exactly which inputs moved the number and why. This is the opposite of a black-box model that returns a score with no explanation, and it is what makes a decision defensible under governance review. The underwriter workbench. Everything surfaces in one interface: the submission dashboard, the documents side by side, the AI summary, the risk signals, and the audit trail of what the AI extracted versus what a human edited. The underwriter spends time on judgment, not on data entry. ‍ The step people miss is that human review lives inside stages two through four, not after them. A managed review team validates the extracted fields and the risk signals before the output reaches the carrier. That is how the accuracy guarantee is possible, and it is the mechanism a pure-AI point solution does not have. ‍ The AI-native underwriting pipeline: submissions flow from intake through extraction, enrichment, and scoring into the underwriter workbench and the policy admin system, with managed human-in-the-loop validation across the stages. ‍ How is AI-native underwriting different from bolt-on AI and BPO? Three architectures are usually on the table. They look similar in a demo and behave very differently in production. The table below is the honest comparison. ‍ Dimension AI-native platform AI bolted onto legacy workflow Offshore BPO Where the AI sits At the center; every document is machine-read first On the side; a feature next to manual forms Nowhere; people key the data New document format Normalized by meaning, no retraining Often breaks; needs a new template or manual keying Handled, but slowly and by hand Accuracy mechanism Model first pass plus managed human validation Model output, then the carrier's team reviews Human double-keying and spot checks Auditability Field-level provenance and edit trail built in Partial; depends on the bolt-on vendor Manual notes, hard to reconstruct What scales Leverage improves as volume grows Review burden grows with volume Cost grows linearly with volume Typical failure mode Exception handling on genuinely novel risks Backlog when formats drift Turnaround stretches to a full day at peak ‍ The two differences that decide the outcome are format handling and leverage. A bolt-on system that depends on templates degrades every time a broker sends a slightly different form, and commercial submissions arrive in dozens of formats. A BPO arrangement is really just a faster spreadsheet: it works, but every additional submission costs another unit of human time, so the economics get worse as you grow, not better. Why does the architecture change the result? Because the constraint in commercial underwriting is not the decision, it is everything that has to happen before the decision. Underwriters are not slow. The data arriving at their desk is slow, incomplete, and inconsistent. When the first pass is manual, the whole line moves at the speed of keying, and adding AI on the side only speeds up the parts that were never the bottleneck. This is a large part of why AI's measured impact on underwriting has lagged other insurance functions : the AI was added to the wrong layer. When the first pass is machine-read and humans validate exceptions, the line moves at the speed of the model, and human effort concentrates where judgment actually adds value. That is the operating leverage. In Pibit.AI's own client data, one workers' compensation MGA program processed 1,053 loss runs and 626 submissions in a single month with zero errors. The number that matters there is not the volume, it is that the underwriting team did not touch the review queue to get it. How should you evaluate AI in underwriting? Most evaluations over-index on the demo, which is the least informative moment because the vendor picked the documents. A better framework asks five questions about the architecture. That framework is deliberately architecture-first, because the architecture is what you are actually buying. The details of how the pipeline is assembled, and how much of it you adopt, are where AI-native platforms differ most from each other, which is the subject of the agentic AI underwriting architecture breakdown. Where does Pibit.AI fit here. Pibit is an AI-native, modular underwriting platform. The CURE platform is five modules: ClearCURE for intake and clearance, DocumentCURE for extraction and normalization, ResearchCURE for enrichment, RiskCURE for scoring, and WorkflowCURE for the underwriter workbench. Carriers adopt them a la carte, most starting with one or two, and the platform sits on top of existing policy admin systems such as Guidewire, Duck Creek, and Insurity rather than replacing them. Accuracy is 99.9% at the field level, committed contractually and backed by a managed review team, which is the reason the accuracy benchmark holds up over time instead of decaying after the pilot. Pricing is a subscription on submissions received, not on policies written. None of that requires ripping out the systems already in place. That is the practical version of AI-native: the AI is at the center of the work, the underwriter is at the center of the decision, and the existing stack stays where it is.

title: The best Airbnb alternatives for UK hosts
summary: Relying on the Airbnb algorithm is a risk. Discover the top alternative booking sites for UK hosts to protect your income and grow your business.
body_text: The best Airbnb alternatives for UK hosts by Guesty Marketing Team | July 20, 2026 Reading time: 5 minutes Share Guesty Marketing Team Share If your entire hosting income depends on the Airbnb algorithm, your business is vulnerable. One temporary listing suspension or a string of unfair reviews can shut you down. Rather than abandoning Airbnb, the most effective strategy is to build a business that’s bigger than one platform by diversifying across multiple booking sites. Listing on alternatives like Vrbo and Booking.com gives you access to millions of new guests, protects your revenue, and reduces your dependency on a single source of bookings. It turns a side hustle into a resilient operation. TL;DR Listing on multiple sites reduces your business risk and insulates you from algorithm changes on any single platform. Different platforms attract different guests: Vrbo for families, Booking.com for international travelers, and niche sites for unique stays. Vrbo is a strong contender for entire homes, often attracting guests who book longer, more profitable stays. Niche UK-focused sites like Sykes Holiday Cottages or Canopy & Stars can connect you with highly motivated domestic travelers. Managing multiple listings requires a channel manager to synchronize your calendars and prevent double bookings. Manual calendar updates using iCal are slow and unreliable, creating a high risk of double bookings. You can manage all calendars, messages, and operations from one central platform. Why UK hosts should list on more than just Airbnb Relying solely on Airbnb is like having a shop on only one street in town. You miss out on all the customers walking down other roads. Expanding to other platforms puts your property in front of new audiences who might never have found you on Airbnb. A multi-channel strategy gives you three distinct advantages: 1. Increased Occupancy: You tap into different pools of travelers. Vrbo is popular with families planning longer holidays, while Booking.com has massive global reach and attracts international and last-minute guests. More visibility means fewer empty nights on your calendar. 2. Higher Revenue: Different platforms have different demand patterns. You might find that guests on a luxury platform like Plum Guide are willing to pay a premium, or that longer stays from Vrbo guests increase your average booking value. 3. Reduced Risk: If your Airbnb account is flagged or your listing’s ranking suddenly drops, your entire income stream is at risk. With bookings coming from multiple sources, a problem on one platform doesn’t cripple your business. You have a safety net. Top Airbnb alternatives for UK hosts compared Each platform serves a different type of traveler. Choosing the right ones for your property depends on your location, style, and the guests you want to attract. Platform Best for Host fee structure (approx.) Key takeaway for hosts Vrbo Entire homes, families, and longer stays 8% (5% commission + 3% payment processing) Attracts guests who plan further in advance and book longer, more profitable stays. Booking.com City apartments, international guests 15% average commission Unmatched global reach, but higher commission fees and you often can’t vet guests beforehand. Plum Guide High-end, design-led properties Membership/vetting fee + commission A curated platform for luxury properties; not for every host, but high revenue potential. Sykes Holiday Cottages Traditional holiday cottages, rural UK Varies (managed service) Strong brand recognition in the UK domestic travel market, especially for classic cottage holidays. Coolstays Unique properties (treehouses, cabins) Annual membership fee A niche platform to attract guests specifically looking for unusual and memorable stays. Canopy & Stars Glamping, cabins, nature-focused stays Commission-based The go-to site for outdoor and eco-conscious travelers; ideal for rural, unique properties. Boost your short term rentals today Get started How to manage listings on multiple sites without double bookings The biggest fear for hosts managing multiple channels is the double booking. You get a reservation on Vrbo. You race to your Airbnb calendar to block the dates, but a new booking comes through before you can. Now you have two guests, one property, and a massive headache that will likely end in a cancellation penalty and a bad review. Manually updating calendars is not a scalable solution. Even iCal syncing is too slow and unreliable , often taking several minutes or even hours to update, leaving a dangerous window for double bookings to occur. The only professional way to manage this is with vacation rental management software . A platform like Guesty® connects to your listings on different channels through a direct API. This direct API provides an instant, two-way connection, avoiding the delays common with iCal syncing. When a guest books your property on Airbnb, a Channel Manager instantly blocks those dates on Booking.com, Vrbo, and any other site you’re listed on. It eliminates the risk of double bookings completely. You can then see all your reservations from every platform in one place. A Multi-Calendar gives you a single view of your availability, so you know exactly what’s happening across your business without logging into three different websites. More channels mean more guest messages. Instead of juggling multiple inboxes, you can manage every conversation from a Unified Inbox . Guesty’s AI agents, like ReplyAI™ , help you handle the increased volume by suggesting or even automating responses based on your rules, ensuring every guest gets a fast, professional reply. FAQ about listing on Airbnb alternatives in the UK Is it worth listing on sites other than Airbnb in the UK? Yes. Diversifying reduces your reliance on a single platform, increases your potential occupancy by reaching new guest demographics, and ultimately builds a more stable and profitable hosting business. What is the most popular alternative to Airbnb in the UK for hosts? Vrbo and Booking.com are the two largest and most popular alternatives. Vrbo is excellent for entire homes and family travel, while Booking.com offers unparalleled access to a global audience, particularly for city-based properties. Can I list my property on Airbnb and Vrbo at the same time? Absolutely. This is one of the most common and effective multi-channel strategies. The key is to use a channel manager to ensure your calendars are always synchronized in real time to prevent double bookings. Which Airbnb alternative is best for properties in London? For London properties, Booking.com is a strong choice due to its popularity with international business and leisure travelers. If your property is high-end and design-focused, applying to be on Plum Guide can attract premium guests and higher nightly rates. How do I avoid double bookings when using multiple sites? Do not rely on manual calendar updates or slow iCal connections. The only reliable method is to use a short-term rental management software with a channel manager. It uses a direct API connection to instantly sync your availability across all your chosen booking platforms the moment a reservation is made. title: Introducing Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.5 Flash Cyber
summary: We’re introducing new Gemini models, including Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.5 Flash Cyber.
body_text: Introducing Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.5 Flash Cyber Jul 21, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Our newest Gemini models deliver the efficiency, latency, and reliability to build AI agents at scale. Tulsee Doshi Senior Director, Product Management, on behalf of the Gemini team Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Developers and customers building production AI agents need higher token efficiency, lower latency, and more reliable performance. Our Flash series of models is built to meet the sweet spot of efficiency and quality to enable scaling agentic workflows. Building on Gemini 3.5 Flash, we’re introducing new Gemini models: 3.6 Flash: Our workhorse model that delivers better coding, knowledge work, and multimodal performance. According to the Artificial Analysis Index , it reduces output token usage by 17% compared to 3.5 Flash, and in some benchmarks like DeepSWE by Datacurve , we observe up to 65%, all at a lower cost per output token. 3.5 Flash-Lite: Our fastest, most cost-effective 3.5-class model, delivering 350 output tokens per second according to the Artificial Analysis Index, also significantly outperforming prior Flash-Lite generations in agentic workflows. 3.5 Flash Cyber in CodeMender: Successful cybersecurity applications require careful orchestration of a model alongside an agent infrastructure. We’re introducing a combination of a new, highly efficient, specialized cyber-focused model paired with our CodeMender code security agent that delivers competitive performance at the frontier. Beyond today’s releases, Gemini 3.5 Pro is currently testing with partners and we plan to make it broadly available as soon as it’s ready. In parallel, our team is already focusing on building the next generation of models. We have started our most ambitious pre-training run yet, for Gemini 4, and are excited by the progress. 3.6 Flash: More efficient and better quality than 3.5 Flash Gemini 3.6 Flash builds directly on developer and customer feedback from 3.5 Flash. 3.6 Flash not only delivers a step up in coding and knowledge work, but it does this while meaningfully improving token efficiency. For example, on the Artificial Analysis Index, we see 3.6 Flash consuming 17% fewer output tokens than 3.5 Flash. It also takes fewer reasoning steps and tool calls to accomplish multi-step workflows. This enhanced efficiency is also combined with a lower price than 3.5 Flash. At $1.50/1M input tokens and $7.50/1M output tokens, 3.6 Flash reduces the overall cost per agentic task, making agents more cost-effective to build and run. 3.6 Flash shows better token efficiency and reduced verbosity than 3.5 Flash in an OSWorld verified task (API) Even while being more efficient, 3.6 Flash sees performance gains compared to 3.5 Flash across use cases: 3.6 Flash delivers higher precision with fewer unwanted code edits and reduced execution loops, as seen in DeepSWE (49% vs. 37%), and shows significant improvement in ML Research, as seen in MLE Bench (63.9% vs. 49.7%). It has improved computer use capabilities as seen in OSWorld-Verified (83.0% vs. 78.4%). Computer use is now a built-in client side tool via the Gemini API and Gemini Enterprise. It outperforms 3.5 Flash in knowledge work, as shown by benchmarks like GDPval-AA v2 (1421 vs. 1349). Customers like Hebbia and Harvey have found it particularly capable at multimodal tasks like document parsing, chart and data analysis, and report drafting. 3.6 Flash, using Managed Agents on AIS, can help parse through and analyze financial data and transcripts more efficiently and accurately than 3.5 Flash (AIS) 3.6 Flash executes code migrations, using multi-agent orchestration on AGY, with lower latency and higher quality than 3.5 Flash (AGY) 3.6 Flash helps develop a photographic texture extractor for 3D workflows, using canvas (Gemini App) 3.6 Flash uses AGY and the tldraw offline editor to build interactive theme studios with its strong visual understanding skills (AGY). Customers report 3.6 Flash is a step forward in both cost and quality, balancing token efficiency, accuracy, and speed across complex workflows and knowledge-based tasks: Built with safety 3.6 Flash is shipping with enhanced Frontier Safety safeguards in the domains of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) and cyber offense misuses. These safeguards make the model substantially more resistant to jailbreaks. At the same time, the model has been trained to minimize refusals for beneficial uses. For more information, see the 3.6 Flash model card. 3.5 Flash-Lite: Built to scale agentic workflows Beyond Flash, we’re also releasing Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, designed for both low-latency tasks and tasks where high throughput is critical for developers workflows, like agentic search and document processing. 3.5 Flash-Lite is the fastest model in the 3.5 series. As measured by Artificial Analysis , it runs at 350 output tokens/s. Priced at $0.3/1M input tokens and $2.5/1M output tokens and with significantly better quality than 3.1 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash-Lite offers a strong price-to-performance ratio for developers and customers running high throughput production traffic. 3.5 Flash-Lite executes high volume tasks at a lower latency than 3.5 Flash. 3.5 Flash-Lite enables efficient scaling for agentic systems. Across thinking levels, the model significantly outperforms 3.1 Flash-Lite. Depending on the workload, developers can configure the model to prioritize low-latency, low-cost execution for high-volume tasks with the minimal and low thinking levels, or engage higher thinking levels to process multi-step subagent workloads. The model now also has computer use as a built-in tool to reliably support these agentic tasks across surfaces. It’s a significant step up in coding and agentic tasks as seen in Terminal-Bench 2.1 (54% vs 31%), long context as seen in GDM-MRCR v2 (72.2% vs. 60.1%), and real-world task execution as seen in GDPval-AA v2 (1140 vs. 642). In fact, on many agentic and coding evals, 3.5 Flash-Lite even outperforms 3 Flash, including on SWE-Bench Pro (54.2% vs. 49.6%) and OSWorld-Verified (74.0% vs. 65.1%), making it a faster & more capable option for workloads on both 2.5 and 3 Flash. 3.5 Flash-Lite extracts product features from a massive e-commerce dataset and synthesizes it. Working alongside 3.6 Flash as the master agent, 3.5 Flash-Lite instantly generates 25 unique, ready-to-explore web design concepts. 3.5 Flash-Lite can scale receipt translation and summarization with its multimodal understanding. 3.5 Flash-Lite builds a game by instantly generating and iterating through multiple options. Early customers of 3.5 Flash-Lite are highlighting its unique combination of speed, intelligence, and cost efficiency for scaling agentic workflows and data processing tasks: For more information about the model, see the 3.5 Flash-Lite model card. 3.5 Flash Cyber in CodeMender: finding and fixing vulnerabilities efficiently AI models have become capable of finding security vulnerabilities faster than current systems can fix them. Tackling this growing threat requires an approach to securing software that is highly capable and efficient. Flash’s performance and efficiency makes it an ideal foundation to detect, validate, and patch code security issues at scale. Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is built on top of 3.5 Flash, and fine-tuned for finding and fixing cybersecurity vulnerabilities at a lower price per token than larger models. Within CodeMender, which uses multiple 3.5 Flash Cyber agents working together to produce a single combined report, 3.5 Flash Cyber reaches competitive performance at the frontier on the popular benchmark CyberGym. Given the dual-use nature of this technology, we have taken an intentional approach to deploying 3.5 Flash Cyber. The model will be exclusively available to governments and trusted partners via CodeMender soon as part of a limited-access pilot program. This will give frontline defenders a head start in finding and fixing critical vulnerabilities before they can be exploited, while mitigating against broader misuse. 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite: Get started today 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite are available starting today: For developers in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio and Android Studio . 3.6 Flash is also available in Google Antigravity . Get started with the Developer Guide . For enterprises in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform . 3.6 Flash is also available in the Gemini Enterprise app . For everyone via the Gemini app . 3.5 Flash-Lite is also rolling out in Google Search. As you start building with 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite, we welcome your feedback to improve future Gemini models and look forward to releasing 3.5 Pro soon.
